entry.title: Dynamic Equilibrium
entry.summary: Balance that looks still but is two flows matched, like a reaction at equilibrium or a body holding its temperature. Control and letting go work this way, and so do sellers and buyers: no one holds the point, both sides keep it.

entry.title: How to Let the Rest Play Out
entry.summary: Letting the rest play out is letting go: full effort on your part, an open hand on the result. In the world but not of it; name the line, count your part as done, act and release, review at the right scale, leave slack.

entry.title: Control, and Letting the World Play Out
entry.summary: Too little control is helplessness; too much makes you fragile. The old split between what is in your power and what is not, observation to tell them apart, and slack to leave room when the world moves.

entry.title: Life, Quarter, Week, Day
entry.summary: Connection, presence and progress are descriptive principles; rewrite them as A over B. Each scale of a life needs its own guidance: principles for a life, strategy for a quarter, rhythm for a week, presence for a day.

entry.title: Happiness Can Be Designed, Partly
entry.summary: A sense of control is called locus of control. Newport’s three needs, and three things that predict a good day: connection, presence and progress. You can design the conditions for happiness, not the feeling.

entry.title: Why an Edge Feels Like Survival
entry.summary: Rank once decided survival, so the brain still treats an edge over others as life or death. What an edge really buys is control, it has no enough, and the urge underneath is security, significance or mastery.

entry.title: Power Is a Means
entry.summary: Power is the currency under most of life’s games, so everyone needs some, and that is why it makes a bad goal. Where it sits among Smoley’s seven games, and why the principle to write down is a definition of enough.

entry.title: Principles Are Guiding Policy for a Life
entry.summary: Rumelt’s kernel of strategy, applied to a life: a diagnosis, a guiding policy and coherent actions. Values are the bedrock, principles the stake, policies the rope; tradeoffs decided ahead of time, and what to check when they stop working.

entry.title: Observation Is a Tool
entry.summary: You shape your tools, then your tools shape you. Observation, used often, becomes a tool, a faculty of attention. Everyone has access to the higher mind; they just need to train their observation on it.

entry.title: Free Up the Higher Mind
entry.summary: Every person has some divinity and some badness, at different levels at different times. Observe how they move you, keep a healthy balance, and automate the routine with habits, rituals and rules so the higher mind has room.

entry.title: Balance Is the Ground, Not the Goal
entry.summary: Devout societies aren’t reliably peaceful; practiced ones are more often. The body wants rhythm, not a fixed point. And most traditions treat balance as the path to the highest things, not the highest thing.

entry.title: Mechanics of a System
entry.summary: The state machine is one of six pictures that hold at every scale. The others are the function, the log, the graph, the queue and the loop. What each one answers, the six questions to ask of any system, and what they leave to cost, people and uncertainty.

entry.title: Modelling State Machines
entry.summary: Most of a syllabus for software systems is one idea: state plus rules, and machines sending messages. One pattern, many substrates, each with its own physics; where the lens stops working; and why AI systems feel different.

entry.title: Arrange Things So You Don’t Need to Know
entry.summary: Taleb’s answer to the need: you can’t know what comes next, so arrange things so you don’t need to. Fragile, robust and antifragile; how smoothing makes us fragile; options, the barbell, via negativa, Lindy and small doses of stress.

entry.title: Is the Need the Core Need?
entry.summary: A hard look at the frame behind these essays. As the first human need, it holds up; as the only one, it doesn’t. Belonging looks just as basic, we seek surprise as well as certainty, and a frame that explains everything needs testing.

entry.title: Manage Commitments, Not Tasks
entry.summary: For ADHD, change the question from how to be productive to what you’ve promised, to whom, and whether you can keep it. The root causes of broken commitments, and how to promise differently, free of tools.

entry.title: Meaning Makes Pain Bearable
entry.summary: Meaning turns pain into a cost paid for something. Viktor Frankl, the soldiers at Anzio and modern pain science, why it works on resistance and on the need, and where it stops being true.

entry.title: Projecting, Masking and ADHD
entry.summary: What we project is a forecast of ourselves. ADHD makes that forecast hard to keep, masking holds it up with a private scramble, and what helps is paying for it in structure instead of effort.

entry.title: What Is Enlightenment?
entry.summary: What are you getting enlightened about? Not a subject. The original words mean waking up and blowing out. Kant’s enlightenment says stop buying your answers; the Buddha’s says see the one who needs them.

entry.title: Bottom-Up Programming for Enlightenment
entry.summary: Paul Graham said to build the language up toward the program. Shinzen Young did that for the mind: six small words for experience, and practices short enough to fit in a sentence.

entry.title: Suffering = Pain × Resistance
entry.summary: Shinzen Young’s formula, and what it would mean for resistance to go to zero: not zero pain, numbness or resignation, but full contact with no fight. The need to know what comes next is the second arrow.

entry.title: Signal or Feature
entry.summary: Every tradition sees that nothing satisfies for long. Is the restlessness a signal of something real we lack, or a feature of how the mind is built? Both fit the evidence, and both agree that nothing you can buy will be enough.

entry.title: Buddhism Through the Lens of the Need
entry.summary: Pleasure is designed not to last, for the same reason uncertainty hurts: the brain is a prediction machine. Buddhism named both sides, craving and aversion, and is the only tradition that treats the need itself as the problem.

entry.title: Answers That Compound
entry.summary: Why buying the answer to the need wins in the moment, and why it loses over time: made answers compound up, bought ones compound down, and the self-made answer has to be built cold for a need that fires hot.

entry.title: Meeting the Need Yourself
entry.summary: How much of the need can you meet without buying it? Most of the core: the boundary, meaning in the act, your own experience library, surprise as material, adapting, putting it outside. Not community, and not death.

entry.title: The Nation as Religion
entry.summary: Run the nation-state through the five questions of The Bundle and it passes almost every test of a religion. It fails two, power and exit, and that makes its fine print the heaviest.

entry.title: The Market for the Need
entry.summary: The need never changes, but the market for it does: four dials, a history from the band to the feed, why religion is now sold in pieces, and what a mass audience is.

entry.title: What Each Religion Sells
entry.summary: Every answer to the need can be read like a product: a problem, a promise, a technique, an exemplar and fine print. The major religions, read that way, and what each one suppresses.

entry.title: The Levers on How You Respond
entry.summary: Eight levers decide how you respond, in the order they act: situation, cues, state and prepared responses before; the gap, attention and meaning during; review after. The earlier the lever, the better it works.

entry.title: The Why Behind the Need
entry.summary: Why all humans need to know what comes next, from the body up: the body pays for not knowing, the brain is built to remove it, the mind will take any answer, and culture answers the biggest one.

entry.title: How Many Responses You Need
entry.summary: If you fix the response instead of the forecast, how many responses do you need? Ashby’s law says enough to match the world, but three escape routes leave about five, plus one default.

entry.title: Know How You’ll Meet It
entry.summary: You can’t know what comes next, but you can know how you’ll meet it. That’s a different answer to the need: fix the response, not the forecast. The Stoics, the Gita, armies, pilots and improv all found it.

entry.title: Culture, Entertainment and the Need
entry.summary: We pay not to know what comes next. Entertainment sells safe uncertainty with an ending guaranteed, culture answers it for everyone at once, the feed removes the ending, and improv answers it differently.

entry.title: Dealing with Anxiety When You Have ADHD
entry.summary: About half of adults with ADHD have had an anxiety disorder, and much of it grows out of the traits. Where it comes from, how to calm it in the moment, and how to make the alarm go off less.

entry.title: Avoid, Detect, Remove Bullshit with ADHD
entry.summary: Bullshit in claims and in systems both come from the need for meaning. ADHD can’t keep up vigilance, so the defense has to be fast, written down, run at a calm time, and removal has to happen by default.

entry.title: Meeting the Need with ADHD
entry.summary: Four parts of the need, four fixes. Not knowing what to do: decide the night before. Faint time: make it visible. Waiting hurts: bring the reward close. Can’t keep a ritual going: automate it.

entry.title: The ADHD Version of the Need
entry.summary: The need for meaning under uncertainty is the same in ADHD, but its time horizon isn’t: the far future pulls less and the next ten minutes pull more. How that works, why the traits survive, and what follows.

entry.title: The Need Is Built In
entry.summary: Why the need for meaning under uncertainty is so strong: how it works in the brain, why evolution built it, and what follows. The need is built in; sellers don’t create it, they sell into it.

entry.title: Why Belief Systems Survive
entry.summary: Hindu chants, kalasams and mudras have a clear internal logic. Most of it was written after the practice, and the whole system grew the way a reef does: no architect, shaped by what survived.

entry.title: Free of Tools
entry.summary: Not the tool with all the features, but the freedom to be free of tools: plain text, picked up anywhere, anytime. For ADHD, the ritual gets done because it’s simple.

entry.title: What I Need, Not What I Can
entry.summary: Obsidian, or any tool like it, is too flexible. Trying to do everything with it, you don’t do what you need. So start with the few jobs you need it for.

entry.title: Not Tools, but Automation
entry.summary: For managing attention, a tool is the wrong shape: it waits for me to remember it. Automation runs on the days I forget.

entry.title: The Automated Morning Brief
entry.summary: One short message every morning, without my asking: the three things for today, the first step, and the fixed times. Why that would help an ADHD brain.

entry.title: The Minimum System for ADHD
entry.summary: Two lists. One with everything. One with what is important now, three items at most.

entry.title: The goal is not a well-organized life
entry.summary: Organizing feels like work, and for a brain like mine it beats the real task every time. So it gets one place, set times, and nothing more.

entry.title: Traditional To-Do Lists Don't Work for ADHD Brains
entry.summary: Traditional to-do lists don't work for ADHD brains. We need focus and structure, not endless tasks.

entry.title: A List of Lists, One Item at a Time
entry.summary: Organize items in a list of lists, but look at them one at a time. Organizing wants to see everything; doing wants to see one thing.

entry.title: What Difference Does ADHD Medication Make?
entry.summary: It turns the noise down. It doesn't choose what to focus on, and it doesn't pick itself up from the pharmacy.

entry.title: Ask a Better Question
entry.summary: Before building a tool, stop and ask what you're trying to achieve and whether there's an easier, quicker or better way. Often that way is a prompt.

entry.title: One Thing at a Time
entry.summary: Do one thing at a time, picked from a short menu, and don't drop it once it's started.

entry.title: How to Build and Test the Best Study Plan
entry.summary: Model memory as chunks and formats as state changes, then test the plan by splitting the subject.

entry.title: Is There a Best Possible Study Plan for a Subject?
entry.summary: No single best plan, but good plans share a structure.

entry.title: Change the Environment to Change the Actions
entry.summary: Change the environment to change the constraints to change the actions, at the right time scale.

entry.title: Constraints Drive Actions
entry.summary: Constraints decide most actions before you decide anything.

entry.title: Removing Bullshit
entry.summary: Most of designing a system is taking things out.

entry.title: Design the Data and the Features Together
entry.summary: Designing the data is designing what the app can do. Design the data and the features together.

entry.title: Own the list, rent the app
entry.summary: Any data structure can be a list. Keep the data in one plain format and change the surface instead.

entry.title: The Spine and the Surface
entry.summary: Keep a small, permanent spine and make everything around it disposable.
